newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weak yen seen driving Japan 96/97 car exports up.
newsitem.headline: Weak yen seen driving Japan 96/97 car exports up.

text.p: Japan's vehicle exports fell in the six months to September for the 10th year in a row, but the weaker yen may help break the long-standing pattern of declining exports for the full fiscal year.
The expected rise in exports for the year ending next March would be the first increase in five years, a car industry body said on Tuesday after releasing the interim export data.
Japan has been exporting fewer cars in recent years as automakers set up factories overseas to mitigate the impact of the strong yen and to move production closer to their markets.
This has resulted in a situation where the carmakers produce more vehicles overseas than they export from Japan.

The Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) said on Tuesday that Japan's vehicle exports in September rose 11.5 percent from the year earlier to 348,623, bringing the cumulative total in the first half of 1996/97 to 1.83 million units, down a scant 0.2 percent from a year before.
It was the fourth straight month that exports had risen on a year-on-year basis. However, in terms of the fiscal first half, it was the 10th year of decline.
The group predicted the full-year figures would show a rise, partly because an auto trade dispute with the United States weighed on last year's figures.

"Japan's exports in the 1996/97 year are sure to exceed last year's 3.62 million units. Exports have been posting gains since June this year because of the weaker yen and lower shipments last year, and they are likely to keep marking gains," a JAMA official said.
The strong car market in the United States and Europe also helped buoy Japan's exports, he added.

Even if exports beat last year's figure, they are still likely to fall far short of the 4.35 million shipped in 1994/95. Japan's vehicle exports in 1995/96 fell a steep 16.7 percent from the year before to 3.62 million units, the fourth straight year of decline.

Japan's exports slackened last year because of a threat of U.S. sanctions before Tokyo and Washington reached a deal to boost foreign access to Japan's car market, as well as the yen's strength. The dollar now stands at around 114 yen compared with around 100 in October last year.
A strong yen hurts the competitiveness of Japanese exporters by making their products more expensive abroad.

JAMA said exports to Asia fell 0.5 percent from a year earlier to 309,577 vehicles in the April to September period, the first decline in two years. Exports to the Middle East marked their first gain in four years with 133,652 units, up 68.9 percent.

Exports to the United States fell 11.5 percent from a year earlier to 544,189 units in April-September, and those to the European Union rose 4.7 percent to 374,194, marking the first year-on-year gain in five years.

In calendar 1995, Japan's vehicle exports fell 15 percent from the previous year to 3.79 million units. This compared with 4.65 million units produced by Japanese car companies overseas, up from 4.22 million in 1994.
